newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia in wrangle over possible mazut export duty.
newsitem.headline: Russia in wrangle over possible mazut export duty.

text.p: Russia is wrangling over whether to introduce a tariff on heavy fuel oil exports, and the cabinet has asked ministries to make recommendations on the matter by December 1, a source close to the issue said on Monday.

Yevgeny Lukashov, a consultant to the Federal Energy Commission, which oversees energy trade issues and is taking part in the tariff debate, said there was heated discussion among government officials over whether mazut exports should be dutied during the colder seasons.
"There are a lot of people for a duty and a lot of people against it," he said. "If it were a simple issue, the decision would have already been taken. But it has not been decided."

He said the matter was being examined by the Fuel and Energy, Economy, Finance and Foreign Economic Relations ministries, as well as by the Federal Energy Commission and various other government bodies.
When asked whether Russia would decide to levy a tariff or not, he said: "It is impossible to say right now."

Trade sources in Moscow and London, worried about vital Russian supplies of heavy fuel oil, have said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will probably sign an order restricting mazut exports by means of a tariff this winter.
A spokesman for the government's press service, which is automatically informed of all signed government decrees, said no such decree had yet been signed.
The State Customs Committee, responsible for enforcing collection of export duties, said it had received no notice that any levy on mazut was forthcoming.
Lukashov said officials were vigorously debating a number of issues pertaining to a possible levy, including well-publicised shortfalls in federal budget revenue.
A tariff could be appealing, because officials are aware the budget is not meeting tax collection targets, which has caused the International Monetary Fund to delay a loan to Moscow.
But a tariff could cause problems because the IMF made Russia scrap all export tariffs by last July as a condition of that loan.
Russia has also quietly reintroduced duties on crude oil exports that many analysts say are the same as the old export tariff.

Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov told Reuters in September an export tariff would be levied but declined to provide details. Deputy Minister Alexander Yevtushenko said in August the duty could be 14 European currency units per tonne.
Russia raised the export tariff on mazut to 16 Ecus per tonne from six Ecus from December 1995 to March 1996 to curb deliveries abroad.
It banned exports of mazut outright from December 1994 to April 1995 over fears of short supplies at home.
